changes.before: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a high-intensity synthetic sweetener.
changes.after: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a synthetic sweetener roughly 200 times sweeter than sugar.

changes.before: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a high-intensity synthetic sweetener. Its molecule contains a cyclic sulphamate structure and provides sweetness with very little mass compared with sugar.
changes.after: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a high-intensity synthetic sweetener, roughly 200 times sweeter than sucrose depending on the food. Because it is so intensely sweet, only a very small amount is needed compared with sugar.

changes.before: Cyclamates are high-intensity sweeteners based on cyclamic acid; Schedule 8 includes the parent acid and its sodium and calcium salts.
changes.after: Cyclamates are intense sweeteners, roughly 30–50 times sweeter than sugar, made from cyclamic acid and its sodium or calcium salts.

changes.before: Cyclamates are high-intensity sweeteners based on cyclamic acid; Schedule 8 includes the parent acid and its sodium and calcium salts.
changes.after: Cyclamates are high-intensity sweeteners based on cyclamic acid. One additive number covers the acid and its sodium and calcium salts.

changes.before: Sucralose is a high-intensity sweetener made by selectively replacing three hydroxyl groups on a sucrose molecule with chlorine atoms.
changes.after: Sucralose starts as ordinary table sugar: three parts of the sucrose molecule are swapped for chlorine atoms to make an intense sweetener.

changes.before: Sucralose is a high-intensity sweetener made by selectively replacing three hydroxyl groups on a sucrose molecule with chlorine atoms. The result is intensely sweet but metabolised very differently from ordinary sugar.
changes.after: Sucralose is made from sucrose through a controlled multi-step chlorination process that replaces three hydroxyl groups with chlorine atoms. The result is intensely sweet, so very small amounts are needed.

changes.before: Neotame is a very high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame but modified so it is far sweeter and behaves differently in the body.

changes.before: Neotame is a very high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame but modified so it is far sweeter and behaves differently in the body.
changes.after: Neotame is a very high-intensity synthetic sweetener, made by chemically modifying aspartame-related amino-acid components and then purifying the result. It is several thousand times sweeter than sucrose, so it is used at extremely low levels.

changes.before: Xylitol is a five-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and vegetables.
changes.after: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol known for the cooling effect it gives sugar-free gum — and it can be made from plant fibre such as wood or corn cobs, or by fermentation.

changes.before: Advantame is an ultra-high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame.
changes.after: Advantame is an ultra-high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame.

changes.after: Advantame is an ultra-high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame. It is made by reacting aspartame-related material with a vanillin-derived intermediate, and the chemical modification dramatically increases its sweetness potency.

changes.before: Choline salts are forms of choline, an essential nutrient-like compound used by the body to make cell membranes and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.

changes.after: Proteases are protein-cutting enzymes. The named examples come from papaya, pineapple and fig-family plants respectively, though other protease preparations can be made by microbial fermentation.

changes.after: Dextrin / roasted starch is ordinary food starch changed by dry heat, which breaks and rearranges some of its long chains.

changes.before: Dextrin / roasted starch is starch that has been dry-heated so some long starch chains break and rearrange. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
changes.after: Dextrin / roasted starch is ordinary food starch changed by dry heat, sometimes with a little acid, without adding a new major chemical group. This makes it perform more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.

changes.after: Starch treatments are chosen for a purpose. For bleached starch that is mainly colour and purity; other modified starches tune stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.

changes.before: Oxidised starch is starch deliberately oxidised to introduce carbonyl/carboxyl groups and reduce chain length.
changes.after: Oxidised starch is food starch that has been deliberately oxidised to change how it behaves when heated, frozen or stored.

changes.after: Oxidised starch is plant starch deliberately oxidised to introduce carbonyl and carboxyl groups and shorten the starch chains. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but the modification makes it perform more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.

changes.before: Enzyme-treated starches is starch whose molecular size or branching has been changed with starch-active enzymes.
changes.after: Enzyme-treated starches are ordinary food starches whose molecular size or branching has been changed using starch-active enzymes.

changes.after: Enzyme-treated starches are starches whose molecular size or branching has been changed with starch-active enzymes. They are deliberately modified so they perform more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.

changes.after: Hydroxypropyl distarch phosphate is starch that has been cross-linked with phosphate bridges and given hydroxypropyl groups — small chemical add-ons.

changes.after: Triethyl citrate is made from citric acid and ethanol and used as a solvent, carrier or plasticiser in specialised food applications.
